corrections.notes: A visual field defect means the craniopharyngioma is symptomatic with chiasmal compromise; surgical management is indicated. Observation is only for asymptomatic lesions.
corrections.source: Endocrine Society/Pituitary Society craniopharyngioma guidance; European Society of Endocrinology craniopharyngioma consensus (2024)
corrections.newExplanation: A bitemporal visual field defect shows that the lesion is already compressing the optic chiasm, so it is symptomatic even if the patient has not noticed it. Surgical resection, aiming for safe maximal removal and decompression of the chiasm, is indicated, with radiotherapy for any residual tumour. Observation is reserved for small, truly asymptomatic lesions with no visual or endocrine compromise. Source: Endocrine Society/Pituitary Society craniopharyngioma guidance; European Society of Endocrinology craniopharyngioma consensus (2024)

corrections.notes: Stereotactic biopsy is not a routine step; histology comes from surgical resection. The crucial pre-treatment step is full endocrine assessment (cortisol, thyroid, DI), as untreated adrenal insufficiency is dangerous perioperatively.
corrections.source: European Society of Endocrinology craniopharyngioma consensus (2024); Endocrine Society/Pituitary Society guidance
corrections.newExplanation: Before definitive treatment of a suspected craniopharyngioma, a full pituitary hormone assessment is essential, including cortisol, thyroid function, growth hormone axis, gonadotrophins and assessment for diabetes insipidus. Untreated adrenal insufficiency or hypothyroidism is dangerous around surgery and must be corrected first. Histology is normally obtained at surgical resection; stereotactic biopsy is not a routine step. Source: European Society of Endocrinology craniopharyngioma consensus (2024); Endocrine Society/Pituitary Society guidance

corrections.newExplanation: For TRAPS with frequent or severe attacks, current EULAR/ACR recommendations favour IL-1 blockade (anakinra or canakinumab) as the targeted treatment of choice; canakinumab is licensed for TRAPS after the CLUSTER trial. Short courses of glucocorticoids can treat individual flares. Etanercept is a second-line alternative, and monoclonal anti-TNF antibodies such as infliximab and adalimumab can paradoxically worsen TRAPS. Source: EULAR/ACR 2021 points to consider for IL-1-mediated autoinflammatory diseases (Romano et al, Ann Rheum Dis 2022); CLUSTER trial (De Benedetti et al, NEJM 2018)

corrections.stemFix: A 62-year-old immunocompetent male is diagnosed with cryptococcal meningitis after presenting with chronic headache and confusion. CSF India ink stain was positive, and cryptococcal antigen was detected. According to current IDSA guidance, what is the recommended induction and consolidation therapy for this patient?
corrections.newExplanation: For cryptococcal meningitis in HIV-negative, non-transplant (including immunocompetent) hosts, IDSA recommends induction with amphotericin B plus flucytosine for at least 4 weeks, extended to 6 weeks if there are neurological complications. This is followed by fluconazole 400-800 mg daily for 8 weeks as consolidation, then 200 mg daily for 6-12 months. Lifelong maintenance is not needed in immunocompetent patients. Source: IDSA Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Management of Cryptococcal Disease (Perfect et al, 2010)

corrections.newExplanation: An afebrile patient with local purulence and erythema but no systemic signs has a mild-to-moderate diabetic foot infection, which can usually be treated orally. NICE suggests co-amoxiclav for moderate infection. Intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam is reserved for severe infection with systemic toxicity or failure of oral therapy, and it does not cover MRSA. Source: NICE NG19 diabetic foot infection antimicrobial prescribing; IDSA diabetic foot infection guideline 2012

corrections.notes: Routine 'total thyroidectomy plus RAI' for all PTC is outdated. ATA 2015/NICE NG230 offer hemithyroidectomy or total thyroidectomy depending on size/risk, with RAI guided by risk stratification. Update option A.
corrections.source: 2015 ATA Management Guidelines for Thyroid Nodules and Differentiated Thyroid Cancer; NICE NG230 Thyroid cancer (2022)
corrections.newExplanation: Surgery is the primary treatment for papillary thyroid carcinoma. For low-risk tumours of 1-4 cm without nodal or extrathyroidal spread, either hemithyroidectomy or total thyroidectomy is acceptable; larger or higher-risk tumours need total thyroidectomy. Radioactive iodine is no longer routine for every patient: it is guided by postoperative risk (generally for high-risk disease, selectively for intermediate risk). Levothyroxine suppression alone, observation of a confirmed cancer and primary external beam radiotherapy are not appropriate. Source: 2015 ATA Management Guidelines for Thyroid Nodules and Differentiated Thyroid Cancer; NICE NG230 Thyroid cancer (2022)

optionEdits.after: Thyroid surgery (hemithyroidectomy or total thyroidectomy depending on tumour size and risk features), with radioactive iodine decided by postoperative risk stratification

corrections.notes: Patient is actively bleeding with platelets 45 and low fibrinogen. BCSH 2009 advises FFP, cryoprecipitate/fibrinogen and platelets in bleeding DIC while the underlying cause is addressed. Treating metastatic cancer isn't an initial ED step.
corrections.source: BCSH guidelines for the diagnosis and management of DIC (Levi et al, Br J Haematol 2009); ISTH harmonised DIC guidance 2013
corrections.newExplanation: Treating the underlying cause is the cornerstone of DIC management, but a patient who is actively bleeding needs blood-component support straight away. BCSH advises fresh frozen plasma for bleeding with prolonged PT/APTT, cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate when fibrinogen is low, and platelet transfusion if platelets are below 50 x 10^9/L. Heparin is for thrombosis-predominant DIC, not active bleeding. Source: BCSH guidelines for the diagnosis and management of DIC (Levi et al, Br J Haematol 2009); ISTH harmonised DIC guidance 2013
